newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Conference lays ground to end child labour scourge.
newsitem.headline: Conference lays ground to end child labour scourge.

text.p: Delegates at an international conference on child labour voiced cautious optimism on Thursday that the battle against the exploitation of the world's 250 million child workers was being won.

"It may be controversial to say it, but I think it can be stated that the battle against child labour is being won," said Assefa Bequele, director of the working conditions department of the International Labour Organisation (ILO).

Bequele was speaking on the final day of the Amsterdam Child Labour Conference, which has focused on the most intolerable types of child labour -- slavery, forced labour and the use of children in prostitution, pornography and drug trafficking.
The 200 government ministers, union leaders and working childrens' representatives at the conference started technical workshops on key areas in the debate over child exploitation.

Under discussion were improving international and regional cooperation, the relationship between globalisation and economic liberalisation and child labour, and a proposed new ILO convention to ban the worst forms of exploitation by 1999.
The two-day conference has called for an immediate end to such practices and it hopes the discussions will start to lay the groundwork for a worldwide ban.
A follow-up conference will be held in Oslo in October to draft an international commitment to eradicate all child work.
Delegates have said this may now be possible because of a sea-change in attitudes to the problem throughout the world.

"Those of us who remember what the situation was like a decade ago, remember a few individual voices crying in the wilderness," Bequele said. "But now the issue has jumped to the top of the international agenda."

Developing nations, where most child labour is concentrated, have long been suspicious of Western interference in the area of workers' rights, fearing this will undermine their main comparative advantage in world trade -- cheap labour.
Indian Labour Minister M. Arunachalam said on Wednesday that the West needed to understand the plight of poverty-stricken families.
"Parents send children away to work instead of sending them to school not because they want it, but because there is no option or alternative for their biological survival," he said.

Bequele said a broad-based movement against exploitation had now grown up, including many governments, corporations, interest groups and individuals, citing as an example recent successes in Pakistan.
On February 14 labour bodies, sports goods manufacturers and local industrialists agreed to take 7,000 children out of jobs stitching soccer balls in the city of Sialkot.
The scope of the problem remained immense though, he warned, with ILO estimates of 250 million children aged between five and 14 at work probably significantly understating the true total.

A background report prepared for the conference says tens of millions of child labourers are still kept in slavery or under forced labour systems such as debt bondage, where children work to pay off a family obligation.
The commercial sexual exploitation of children has also become a growing concern, it says, with organised networks trading in children both nationally and internationally.
While recognising the complexity of the broader child labour issue, the conference said these sorts of abuses had to be stamped out immediately.

"Where child labour reaches this level, human dignity is at stake and the mental and physical integrity of the child is violated," said Dutch Social Affairs Minister Ad Melkert, who is chairing the conference.
"The flagrant exploitation of children has to be banned. We cannot close our eyes to this problem for one more day."
